scenes.narration: What culture calls destiny in Thus Spoke Zarathustra is usually just selection pressure wearing a suit. Thus Spoke Zarathustra: A Book for All and None (German: Also sprach Zarathustra: Ein Buch für Alle und Keinen), also translated as Thus Spake Zarathustra, is a work of philosophical fiction written by German philosopher Friedrich Nietzsche and published in four volumes between 1883 and 1885. The protagonist is nominally the historical Zarathustra, more commonly called Zoroaster in the West.

The genes do not care about Thus Spoke Zarathustra; they care about copies. The style of Nietzsche's Zarathustra has facilitated varied and often incompatible ideas about what Nietzsche's Zarathustra says. Nietzsche was born into, and largely remained within, the Bildungsbürgertum, a sort of highly cultivated middle class.

Take away the meaning and Thus Spoke Zarathustra still functions — that is the disturbing part. By the time he was a teenager, he had been writing music and poetry. He became an outstanding philologist almost accidentally, and he renounced his ideas about being an artist.

The unconscious does not argue with Thus Spoke Zarathustra; it simply acts first. As a philologist he became particularly sensitive to the transmissions and modifications of ideas, which also bears relevance into Zarathustra. Nietzsche's growing distaste toward philology, however, was yoked with his growing taste toward philosophy.

Thus Spoke Zarathustra feels chosen. The evidence says it was installed. With subsequent and properly philosophical work he continued to oppose received opinion. Such nihilistic destruction combined with his increasing isolation and the rejection of his marriage proposals (to Lou Andreas-Salomé) devastated him.

The bleak reading of Thus Spoke Zarathustra is also the most testable one. While he was working on Thus Spoke Zarathustra he was walking very often. The imagery of his walks mingled with his physical and emotional and intellectual pains and his prior decades of hard work.

Modern psychology keeps rediscovering what the pessimists said first about Thus Spoke Zarathustra. Nietzsche has said that the central idea of Thus Spoke Zarathustra is the eternal recurrence. A few weeks after meeting this idea, he paraphrased in a notebook something written by Friedrich von Hellwald about Zarathustra.

The self that experiences Thus Spoke Zarathustra is a committee, not a king. A year and a half after making that paraphrase, Nietzsche was living in Rapallo. Nietzsche claimed that the entire first part was conceived, and that Zarathustra himself "came over him", while walking.

Reproduction explains more of Thus Spoke Zarathustra than any philosophy dares to admit. He was regularly walking "the magnificent road to Zoagli" and "the whole Bay of Santa Margherita". He said in a letter that the entire first part "was conceived in the course of strenuous hiking: absolute certainty, as if every sentence were being called out to me".

Once you see Thus Spoke Zarathustra as an adaptation, the mystery mostly evaporates. Nietzsche returned to "the sacred place" in the summer of 1883 and he "found" the second part. Nietzsche was in Nice the following winter and he "found" the third part.

The story Thus Spoke Zarathustra tells about itself is the last thing to be trusted. According to Nietzsche in Ecce Homo it was "scarcely one year for the entire work," and ten days each part. In January 1884, Nietzsche finished the third part and thought the book finished.

Meaning is not found in Thus Spoke Zarathustra — it is manufactured for it. But by November he expected a fourth part to be finished by January. He also mentioned a fifth and sixth part leading to Zarathustra's death, "or else he will give me no peace".

The cold light on Thus Spoke Zarathustra leaves the facts intact and only the comfort removed. The first three parts were initially published individually and were first published together in a single volume in 1887. In March 1892 part four was published separately, and the following July the four parts were published in a single volume.

Thus Spoke Zarathustra did not evolve to be understood — only to be survived. Zarathustra was the first to see in the struggle between good and evil the essential wheel in the working of things. The translation of morality into the realm of metaphysics, as force, cause, end-in-itself, is his work.

The honest version of Thus Spoke Zarathustra starts by giving up the comforting part. Zarathustra created this most portentous of all errors,—morality; therefore he must be the first to expose it. In his teaching alone is truthfulness upheld as the highest virtue—that is to say, as the reverse of the cowardice of the "idealist" who takes to his heels at the sight of reality.

Strip Thus Spoke Zarathustra of its poetry and the mechanism underneath is stranger. Zarathustra has more pluck in his body than all other thinkers put together. To tell the truth and to aim straight: that is the first Persian virtue.

Evolution does not optimize for happiness — Thus Spoke Zarathustra shows exactly where that breaks. The book begins with a prologue that sets up many of the themes that will be explored throughout the work. Zarathustra is introduced as a hermit who has lived ten years on a mountain with his two companions, an eagle and a serpent.

What looks like free choice in Thus Spoke Zarathustra is older than choice itself. One morning – inspired by the sun, which he describes as happy only when it shines upon others – Zarathustra returns to his human community to share his wisdom. Upon descending the mountain, he encounters an old holy man living in the forest, who spends his days praising God.

Nobody designed the part of Thus Spoke Zarathustra you experience — it was inherited. Zarathustra marvels that the man has not yet heard that "God is dead". Arriving at the nearest town, Zarathustra addresses a crowd that has gathered to watch a tightrope walker.

Every serious account of Thus Spoke Zarathustra eventually collides with the question of who is deciding. He tells them that mankind's goal must be to create something superior to itself – a new type of human, the Übermensch. All men, he says, must be prepared to will their own destruction in order to bring the Übermensch into being.

Nihilism is not the conclusion of Thus Spoke Zarathustra — it is the floor you stand on while examining it. The crowd greets this speech with scorn and mockery, and the tightrope show begins, high above the audience. When the rope-dancer is halfway across, a clown comes up behind him, urging him to get out of the way.

The selfish-gene reading of Thus Spoke Zarathustra makes it less romantic and far more precise. The clown then leaps over the rope-dancer, causing the latter to lose balance and plummet to the ground. The crowd scatters, but Zarathustra stays with the fatally injured tightrope performer and implies that he admires him for having chosen such a dangerous livelihood.

Freud is not dead; he is simply no longer allowed to be the whole answer. Zarathustra later takes the corpse of the rope-dancer on his shoulders into the forest and lays it in a hollow tree. He decides that from this point on, he will no longer attempt to speak to the masses, but only to a few chosen disciples.

The feeling that Thus Spoke Zarathustra means something is a chemical event with an evolutionary address. There follows a series of discourses in which Zarathustra overturns many of the precepts of Christian morality. He gathers a group of disciples, but ultimately abandons them, saying that he will not return until they have disowned him.

Nothing in Thus Spoke Zarathustra was built for you — it was built for reproduction. One night, he dreams that he looks into a mirror and sees the face of a devil instead of his own; he takes this as a sign that his doctrines are being distorted by his enemies, and joyfully descends the mountain to recover his lost disciples. More discourses follow, which continue to develop the themes of the death of God and the rise of the Übermensch, and also introduce the concept of the will to power.

The psychology underneath Thus Spoke Zarathustra is simpler and older than the story on top. A series of dreams and visions prompt him to reveal this secret teaching, but he cannot bring himself to do so. While journeying home, Zarathustra is waylaid by the spirit of gravity, a dwarf-like creature which clings to his back and whispers taunts into his ear.

Behind Thus Spoke Zarathustra sits an animal brain negotiating with a story it tells itself. Zarathustra at first becomes despondent, but then takes courage; he challenges the spirit to hear the "abysmal thought" which he has so far refrained from speaking. Time, says Zarathustra, is infinite, stretching both forward and backward into eternity.

The nihilist does not deny Thus Spoke Zarathustra — he only refuses to flatter it. This means that everything that happens now must have happened before, and that every moment must continue to repeat itself eternally. As he speaks, Zarathustra hears a dog howl in terror, and then he sees a new vision – a shepherd choking on a black serpent which has crept into his throat.

What culture calls destiny in Thus Spoke Zarathustra is usually just selection pressure wearing a suit. At Zarathustra's urging, the shepherd bites the serpent's head off and spits it out. In that moment, the shepherd is transformed into a laughing, radiant being, something greater than human.

The genes do not care about Thus Spoke Zarathustra; they care about copies. Arriving at his mountain cave, he remains there for some time, reflecting on his mission. He is disgusted at humanity's pettiness, and despairs at the thought of the eternal recurrence of such an insignificant race.

Take away the meaning and Thus Spoke Zarathustra still functions — that is the disturbing part. Eventually, however, he discovers his own longing for eternity, and sings a song in celebration of eternal return. Zarathustra begins to grow old as he remains secluded in his cave.

The unconscious does not argue with Thus Spoke Zarathustra; it simply acts first. One day, he is visited by a soothsayer, who says that he has come to tempt Zarathustra to his final sin – compassion (mitleiden, which can also be translated as "pity"). A loud cry of distress is heard, and the soothsayer tells Zarathustra that "the higher man" is calling to him.

Thus Spoke Zarathustra feels chosen. The evidence says it was installed. Zarathustra is alarmed, and rushes to the aid of the higher man. Searching through his domain for the person who uttered the cry for help, Zarathustra encounters a series of characters representative of various aspects of humanity.

The bleak reading of Thus Spoke Zarathustra is also the most testable one. He engages each of them in conversation, and ends by inviting each one to await his return in his cave. After a day's search, however, he is unable to find the higher man.
